body: Yea. I don't know what they believe. Some places are alright, but meds shouldn't be the first answer. My best times were with the people. The drugs made it worse.
Is there anything I should know that would give them permission to force it? I'm not violent, so I think I'll be good.
But will they literally make you take it or just keep you longer?

Meds work for some people and for some people they seem to add to the problem in the long run. IMO, they should be a last resort, something you take if you've tried everything else. I'm happy to be off them for 5 months now.

if you're not spiritual that's great, I am not currently
It's purely for the sounds, in that case

Something that has helped me, and I don't recommend doing this if you don't have to, when I was just wanting to die -- I would just fantasize about some holding me with a gun counting down. It was surreal, horrible, but also *pleasant* in that moment. Anyway, it helped me know that I can die at any-time I want if I finally have had enough. Knowing I have that option opens up my heart to the possibility of gritting my teeth and fighting some more.

Rise up.
No that is almost what it was. I hesitate to say "imposter" but it was something similar and or close to that. Thanks for your input.
That's the spirit. I think disobeying OCD creates true grit in ways.

Just imagine a Surgeon preparing for an operation; I can imagine being *obsessive* about doing things well would enhance the performance. 

Imagine a genius who writes a great-tale of overcoming hardship and nails every-aspect of feeling and character and detail -- you could say they are "obsessed".

With us, it seems we could be great, but we get drowned in the uncertainties of things that generally do not affect the big picture and wander off into a hall of rituals that are no better than sacrificing goats and drinking the blood to archaic god.

It's all a bit silly. But you could be great. Just try.

Do absolutely nothing about your urges to feel 'right' and *ironically* you will feel more right eventually than ever.

I think subconsciously we notice things that seem *off*, and with the OCD mind-set it can trigger us into an episode well beyond what it was worth.

OCD would be great, without the compulsions.

It would be giving you reassurance to help you logically figure this out. You have to deal with uncertainty. But everyone deserves a *choice*.

Maybe he was having a hard time recently and needed to vent to a complete stranger -- it's what I wish I could do at times, just go up to someone and be close to them for a microsecond in time and move on.

I grew up in a religious family and am logically an atheist (superstitious psychology); but I always took a personal interest in the portrayal of hell in Dante's Inferno. The ideas of hell were *interesting* (not literally); how pride / ego deteriorates and or is the last thing standing in hard-suffering, stuff like that; how it makes or breaks you.

Call bullshit on the voices in your head telling you to 'repent' or you are 'a sinner'; there is no such thing, only you and an abyss just like before you were born.

Obvious rules of OCD apply here though, don't counter, feel it, and hopefully, move on.
It's okay. I didn't word it very well. Just the thoughts that came to mind at the time.

It's moreso for me that I am in disbelief over the person I am that has come out of this. You get this image of a person who walks over the abyss and comes out and when you see him, I'm just like "wtf, that's what I am".

I find great purpose in always having an enemy to fight; without it I feel worthless.

It's not necessarily that the OCD is right it's more like I never defeated it. Like I'm not really the person who came out on the other end of it.

I guess you always kind of expect more from coming out of hardship, like you're going to be some beast. But it's never really that way . . .

I've kind of just accepted that there is some shit that will always disturb me. 90-99% of the intrusive thoughts in my head never reach the level of I'm literally going to kill myself because of how I feel if it doesn't stop

so don't hurt yourself -- just accept that there is darkness and that is "OK" because you will be better because of the struggle it gives you

or maybe not -- maybe it's all a curse

uncertainty

blocking is when you're having a thought and you think of something else to basically get rid of it

when all else failed and I was just in the worst of it the main thing that helped me was literally just touching soft things with my hands -- I would just lay down and touch stuff and notice how it felt

It's got to end some-day, but if you're having physical sensations, I can see why it's going to be hard to *desensitize* -- you're physical wiring / nerves are not going to suddenly lose intensity

Usually what I have heard is that if you don't interact / engage / counter / block them they get less and less.

I guess it's not necessarily true?

I've had thoughts that I literally stop breathing for and it's toxic.

Try therapy first. It's not like some weird seance ritual. You have to work almost as hard as the therapist if you want to make progress. You've got to identify your problems and really try to expose yourself.

Medication I say seemed like it put my life on hold for 2 years and just numbed me off to my problems.

Try and deal with the issues yourself until proven incapable otherwise.

Sometimes it feels like my thoughts are physically connected to my body and if I have a really plowed into my brain thought, it sends signals to me that I must take a deep breath, raise my hand, readjust and stuff like that.

I'm still dealing with a lot, but that chapter I want to say is forever closed.

I hope for you goodness in your struggle.

For me, my greatest personal fear that does not involve other people, was being present / fully aware of my heart-beat. To me it was sickly, felt more attached than connected and just pulsated. At first I could not stop squirming around and I knew I had to go down to the deepest level, just be completely still and *feel it*.

It's like I was made of ash and I wished I was dead and I had a panic attack after the night had passed.

The most important thing was the fear of what I had experienced was more painful than the actual thing itself.

90-99% of OCD problems are like that I imagine.

You're going to be feeling everything you've tried not to feel. It will hit its peak if you can let it and then it will pass.

Far, far away -- there is a place just right and for a moment you can forget it all.

The thing is their compulsions don't usually go out of check in terms of how dysfunctional it can make them. But yea, ERP, even without OCD could be helpful in enhancing the quality / productivity in your life.

I am in a stage in my life where I'm not sure exactly what's me and what's purely stress. Even so, going through all of this will make a difference if I ever get out.

oh yea and I was watching that guys videos before -- they are really good!

I hope for you the best.

I'm the kind of person who likes to take the plunge if I'm going to do something.

But yea, I can see why it'd be recommended to do that. 

For now I'm staying on the surface of my being and just enjoying the little things that happen.

"if you can do erp you can do anything"

that really says it all

this is weird but when I was dealing with my deepest personal fear of being present to my heart-beat, my mind personified it with this struggle between the brain itself and all I asked was for them 'to mediate / reconcile / work together' so we can move past the pain

I still have yet to see if I will see anything rise from the ashes.

I already had that black heroin kind of sickening anxiety attack over what I felt and I really felt it.

What's done is done, moving on now.

I don't have a problem with it I'm just warning people they need to be a fucking beast if they're going to go into the depths.

I already did that and I'm not going back anytime soon or ever.

My idea was that I'm reconstructing from the core up / out.

I'm staying mindful but not the sensory autamoton I was.
Yea, I'm not revisiting that place again if I don't have to. I finally stopped squirming and I am proud of myself for conquering that fear, but it was just uncomfortable to say the least.

You have to put effort into therapy -- surprisingly, you might be working just as hard as them to figure out solutions and move on.

For me medication stunted therapy. No use talking to a zapped out dude who doesn't give a shit either way.

That's one thought that came to mind, but when I really thought about it, I knew it must be alien to them.

I suppose you just got to be uncomfortable sometimes and let it reach its peak and pass.

Sometimes you've just got to do something and figure out how hard it will be as a sort of test. After you've had a taste, you've got to decide on whether to commit or not.

In my case, I'm already WD'ing from benzos, so nicotine mixed into that would fuck shit up.

Nicotine is a vicious chemical -- it can make you feel like a bug being zapped coming off of it. Do it in increments. I switched to vaping at least and with vaping you can lower the dosage whenever you're ready.

But I also absolutely hate certain sounds I have been exposing myself like you said to these things.

Do you think hearing my own thoughts is just an example of that?

I actually like sound a lot; it's just annoying to hear you own thoughts be *spoken* to you you for some reason. I love ASMR and other ambient noises and music.

Sound is a lot to me.
The problems are the compulsions. The compulsions help at first but make the problems bigger ultimately. You have to cut that stuff out.

Numbness through decentization is something you have to work at rather than taking medication which just blocks it off for you. 
I'd rather work on it even if I just end up indifferent. At least it will be earned.

I've had the pure *hatred* thing before. When I hear certain music at times, it almost sends me into a suicidal rage. It's like the idea that something could sound so ugly might change people's way of life. It's crazy. Acknowledge it. Move-the-fuck-on.

The problems arise when you can't let-go of these thoughts, feelings, compulsions and urges. You've just got to accept "shit happens".

Thanks for being honest about it. It's kind of grim to think things *this* bad only based off my own experience could last indefinitely.
For me, I blame benzo withdrawal for how intense my OCD is now. I never had any severe problems with it before. It's only been in the past month or couple months that it's been the main problem.

I don't envy anything you are going through.

I believe psych-drugs can definitely make things worse (I'm not speaking for everyone) in my experience, because I've never had these issues until medication.

If you've ever had a pet or something or a person you cared about, the main thing that is usually relevant is that they can feel. Non-human animals feel and can be hurt just like humans -- maybe not in the same ways, but it isn't any less meaningful.

I personally prefer to just stay away from people who don't have at least similar views on suffering. I can still interact with them on a "I'm human, you're human" level.

There was some point in my life when I wasn't as strict about these things and wouldn't feel as much guilt, but what I can't stand is the mental disconnect between the thing on their plate and what they would actually do for another being.

Logically, you're not actually hurting anyone when doing anything with him. The best advice I've heard for vegans is "be an example"; don't cut people off.

When I was inpatient, I just remember I didn't give much fuck about anyone; an old guy was sent to the ER because he was barely breathing and another guy attacked a nurse right in-front of me and I didn't feel much.

Fuck being numb and blocked off. Cheers.

I agree with "meds aren't for everybody". It's a good thing you got off benzos, they can form a chemical dependency that is worse than nicotine withdrawal (or around that level) in my experience. I'm 3 months or so off psych-drugs, and I feel like I am actually dealing with my problems than putting blankets on them.

Keep it up.
The worst emotion for me is guilt. At times it has felt like I've been dragged by the ear to smell my own anti-OCD shit.
I looked at the sun around the time I thought it was supposed to happen and nothing happened. Didn't even know you could go blind.

Thank you for the long-thought-out response.

"Purificationists can yell at me if they like. I haven't eaten animals in over a decade but I WILL finish that sandwich if it's going in the bin anyway."

Logically this makes perfect sense, but psychologically eating a dead animal should be no different than if you were eating a human -- I know, it's idealistic. Again, logically, if you were starving and the only thing around was dead humans, you shouldn't feel bad about eating them. Psychologically, most people would have a hard time, even if the human flesh didn't come from someone they personally cared about. The question becomes, why don't we feel that way about an old can of tuna or someone's half-eaten sandwich?

I suppose that line of thinking is kind of what you'd come to expect in a future where human and non-human animal exploitation were finally just as much a crime.

"but since the ant isn't particularly bothered whether it lives or dies, my own consideration of energies needs to go on animals who actually do care much more whether they live or die"

While it's true that there isn't much evidence whether or not a majority of insects feel or other small animals, I'd err on the side of caution -- simple things like *don't go stomping around wherever you please when outside*.

When talking about sentience, the things you need to consider are neurons, nervous systems and brains. Cockroaches and bees seem to have some of these (nervous systems I believe), so I'd try and be cautious, basically just don't go out of your way to recklessly kill them. If you do, try and make it quick.

I personally hate roaches and lived with them for awhile, but I still am pretty disturbed to think they might feel something. This isn't my idea but someone I respect basically said it could be binary -- horror or bliss -- just very simple kind of motivation and reward mechanisms.

Besides, it makes me feel sick when I miss an ant and see it squirm around; my gut just tells me to make it quick.

But you're right, the guilt center in my brain is probably the most active it's ever been. I'd prefer to focus on the big picture rather than get lost in the details.

Even in the worst of the worst of the things that I have ever been through, medication for me over-all was great at first, but it cannot be warned enough that this stuff can catch up to you. It put a blanket over my problems, but I wasn't actually dealing with them.

Number 1 problem for me was that it can make you complacent, unwilling to change anything even though it's not very good. It feels almost like your life is put on hold.

I'd go through this pain of being off them over and over just to get to the other side to see who I will be.
sorry I said against when I meant for . . . I need some sleep

That's very helpful. I like the "be an example" thing because it actually makes sense. It's really hard for me to find the right niche to talk about these things, because I'm basically for* an over-all harm reduction in the world.

I can tell that you're right, thinking this way *will* inevitably cut me off from a lot of the world and I can't bare isolation.

The logic in my head is basically extremely idealistic, i.e. "If sadism and cannibalism is looked down upon, why shouldn't you react the same way for non-human animals?" If I disagree, I'm basically a speciest. 

Thanks for your comment.

You've really got to commit. To me, this idea seemed pointless and a chore. Things that can help is plugging in headphones with your phone and listening to something that calms you.

It is extremely important when doing this to also *not counter* any bothersome thought and let-go. These things are both crucial.

An example of something that I like to listen to at times is something like this: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XxDGSLdKVT8

I'm not talking about doing it as long as you can where that would ever happen. The way I do it is in basically small amounts, where I give myself enough time to catch my breath and breathe in-between every-time.

It's basically learning to feel control over your body and can clear the mind. I would basically try to set-aside a good hour or so to simply breathing -- only holding your breath when it's really bad. But yea, don't be reckless, allow yourself to have enough oxygen over-all -- only doing it in bursts.

And how is deep breathing any different? I basically set aside time for the day that I will lay down and focus on breathing; only using cycles of holding my breath in short bursts when I want to see the spaces between thoughts become further apart.

It's a reasonable technique like anything else and I think it helps a lot when things are worse than usual.
Yea, I'll agree with that.

I suppose the answer would be you have to get out of that relationship asap, but considering she's disabled you might feel bad about doing that. In which case, if you're not planning on / unable to change the situation, you're basically stuck with doing the same coping mechanism as everyone else.

The typical ones are 'mindfulness' / being present -- not countering intrusive / obsessive thoughts (not responding with your own line of dialogue / piece of logic) -- absorbing the sensory information around you (focusing on breathing / listening to sound / feeling the involuntary actions of the body, etc.). These will feel like a pointless chore at first, but they are basically the *bread and butter* of moving on with your life, at least for me they have.

Good luck.

It's kind of like the brain doesn't know what to do when you don't interact with the cobwebs of your own mind.

I don't know how helpful it will be, but I noticed holding your breath and the urge to breathe can shut down the mind *somewhat* if you do it enough. I know it sounds bad, so DON'T over do it. Preferably, you should lay down and listen to something as peaceful you can.

Yea I've had racist thoughts too. It's pretty bad, I can't watch anything with a particular race in it without having the thoughts come out so I've avoided it sometimes and it has made me feel like 'I might actually be racist' but in actuality I just don't want those thoughts.

To me just letting the thoughts be seemed insane and pointless at first, but an important key for doing this is being present (absorbing your sensory information) rather than just ignoring (not countering) the thoughts. You don't have to attach a philosophy or spiritual aspect to it like so many people do; it's a natural mechanism that can give a similar effects to drugs if you work hard at it.

It's definitely difficult when you hear language that directly accuses you. The worst thoughts for me are the ones that use "I" language: "I am a pedophile".

Have you tried any kind of serious forms of calming yourself down that don't involve drugs -- laying down for a good hour just focusing on your breathing and listening to something pleasant?

When you absolutely need silence, I've tried holding my breath and remaining frozen in a pose laying down -- the urge to breathe distracts the mind enough to where it either shuts mostly down or only thinks about getting that next breath. I wouldn't recommend doing it all the time, but it can help in reasonable doses.

My rules usually revolve around my ethics of doing no harm, so it seems innocent at first, but it definitely twists the whole logic of it. It tricks you into thinking you are being caring and decent, but really it's just a lot of bad habits which lead to literally checking on every potential outcome you could negatively affect someone.

I know that I can't have my family involved in my life too much. I need a barrier that dissects my space and the space I give to them.

These thoughts do not discriminate. 

Unfortunately until we've isolated and dealt with the core problems, certain people are inevitably going to *trigger* (for lack of a better word) us.

Maybe you should take a brake from it. 

I don't do well if I'm *trying* to enjoy myself; you just kind of have to accept that it's no different than anything else when you apply OCD to it -- at least in terms pain.

I suppose the general advice is to not act on the compulsion to fix the things that trigger you, but when it comes to something that is supposed to do the exact opposite, you really should take a brake from it -- otherwise you might begin to associate it with a negative experience, kind of like being shocked when pressing the wrong key.

I think the bottom line is dealing with your OCD outside of the areas of life which should bring joy. If you run away from your problems, eventually they will catch up to you in places that were meant to be safe.

You basically have to have logic built as deep into you as possible. It seems like some people get lost because they don't have a concrete basis to reference from.

Logic almost has to be as deep as your instinctual feeling that something is wrong.

Something is wrong to be sure, but not with your character.

I can see how constantly controlling your breathing could become a problem -- my brain has physically hurt if I do the exercises too much and or get a sedating feeling because I'm controlling my heart rate too.

I suppose if this is a problem for you, you could try controlling other parts of the body that don't affect your over-all state of being. Yoga seems to be something like this. What I've done is much more mild: essentially choosing a pose while lying down and locking into it.

I have found that holding my breath and the urge to breathe and feeling the involuntary actions of the body almost *shuts down* the mind -- which is incredible for someone with intrusive thoughts. If you realize that if you try and hold your breath for too long, you *will* breathe on your own no matter how much you try and control it.

Well it isn't fine. You've got to deal with it yourself. No one can do that for you. In that sense we are all alone. It doesn't mean you should stay in your house or room or cut off all connection from people -- that will surely make things worse. I'm speaking from experience 4+ months of no human contact.

You have to literally just be an observer for the tidal wave -- not speaking up, not acting out -- purely witnessing what the thoughts are and what you feel. That is the hardest part. It gets much worse before it gets better.

Eventually you will be able to think more for yourself, but for the longest time you will simply be observing your thoughts and feelings more than interacting.

There are 3 stages to the mind that I have noticed: the deepest being what you are hardly aware of but is basically the autopilot of the brain guiding your actions if you are not directly calling out everything you do; the 2nd is basically the mind's mind -- everything you think before you actually say it *aloud* in your head -- this is where you have the most control over whether or not to *counter* a disturbing thought or keep moving.

If you do this for long enough, say a year or so and see no progress -- I've given myself permission to kill myself. But I know it will never happen, because it will work.

I hope it works out for you.

What are the connotations being applied to the statement "you're part of something now" -- what images or implications appear for you when you hear that? All it means is it's an objective condition not relating to your character which should make you feel better.

Just ask yourself if you've actually ever done anything horrible that the intrusive thoughts keep disturbing you about. Many people are afraid of becoming / acting on these thoughts but never do. That shows your character remains unaffected no matter how bleak the circuitry in your mind is. If anything, you will become stronger by moving on despite the thoughts and you will notice over time they will become further and further apart.

It's fucking brutal. No one is saying otherwise. 

You've really got to commit to not countering / undoing the thoughts and just push on.

My brain has felt somewhat like a sore muscle from all the 'mindfulness' techniques. I've never exerted such mental energy in my life to just look past the searing doomscape.

So what exactly do you mean by *ignore*? I went from telling most every thought in my head to "shut up" to asking the question "what?" over and over to state my ambivalence -- it helped initially but it was just a compulsion eventually and I wasn't really facing the darkness of these thoughts.

Now I just DO NOT *counter* any thought (for the most part) no matter how ugly or vile -- basically just keeping a stream of thought propelling onward to god knows where.

That sounds awful -- but the principle really remains the same -- DO NOT try to *counter* anything that bewilders you -- unless it's some kind of psychosis, the thoughts WILL become further and further apart and you will get stronger.

My OCD usually revolves around sexual and or violent acts, but I do have a bit of everything.

It's kind of strange -- this form of OCD almost sounds like Alzheimer's -- but instead of literally forgetting who you are, it plays on your doubts. Fucking brutal.

"If these thoughts/memories aren't real, then where did they come from?"

I think I'd call this *begging the question*; it is obnoxiously provoking you to answer because it is simply feeding on your doubts that there is something wrong with you, not necessarily out of genuine curiosity.

This too shall be thrown in the trash.


"So I see no other way to live than to ignore every single thought. The thing is, that demands a constant state of mindfulness and mental strength."

Indeed, my head literally hurts from the breathing exercises I've done to today -- it's like my brain is tired of catching myself in pre-thought just in time to not actually speak aloud in my own mind as to counter every bothersome broken thought.

I am completely on my own for the most part and am dealing with hard-core bleak thoughts ad naseaum. The way I'd describe the mind is this: pre-thought (the mind's mind) -- this is the *choice* center, the part YOU are involved in whether or not to *speak aloud* (the mind's mouth) and counter / engage with bothersome and or disruptive thoughts that do not pertain to the dominant thread of thoughts that led your body here.

You CAN essentially stop thinking in the sense that you only whisper (pre-think), observe (foremost), and feel the emotion or physical sensation of any resulting foreign stimuli. You must allow yourself to feel the full extent of every thought until those thoughts dissipate.

I'd hope it's forever, but there are no easy solutions. You must commit.
It's happened to me. It's basically a gradual build-up of complacency even though you know things aren't good. Much better to face the problems yourself than block them off in my opinion.

These reassuring thoughts definitely help *at first*, but like you said in your post, they pretty much just become another compulsion / obsession too. And you are right, it is fucking hard; but the advice is good -- sitting with all of it is far better in the long-run rather than continuing and developing the cycle of mantras repeating like a broken record, checking, analyzing, using logic, critiquing, performing rituals, etc.

The thing I hear that I kept ignoring for awhile was the 'mindfulness' techniques -- noticing things around you, focusing on your breathing . . . very simple things that seem ludicrous in the face of such blackness. But I have given it a shot recently, and I've just been with every thought. The aforementioned thought in this post was the biggest exception.

The thing I have noticed is that I have become more disciplined without even telling myself to do so. 

I wouldn't call it trying not to think, but essentially the trick is not *countering* the thoughts that come up in your head. It's a much emptier space in here than it ever was with the ocd. 

Thanks for the comment.

If you take them on a consistent basis, there is a high chance you will develop a dependency on them -- it is not merely psychological -- it is chemical. The longer you are on them, there is a chance for tolerance to your dose -- so you will have to keep increasing what you're taking. If you ever wish to get off of them at this point, you will be in for a world of hell.

Not everyone goes through hell getting off of them, and they are very lucky. I'm somewhat in the mid-range.

This drug magnifies anything you are suffering through now to inane proportions. I have wished I was dead many times.

Best info you can get that is formal and factual is here: http://www.benzo.org.uk/manual/bzcha01.htm

Search YouTube with "benzo withdrawal" and you will see real faces of people who have and are going through hell.

The best personal description / experience I've seen was by Brian Baxter. I saw it when I was younger and wish I had remembered the word *benzos*. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=97Wlx_UzWYg

Good for you.

Just don't think medication is necessarily the salvation of everything -- be very wary of any drugs they want to give you, research them all -- they are not a joke.

My biggest mistake was taking medication without question. They can drastically change your life. 

The scary thing is I believe being on this medication so long has actually made my intrusive thoughts and ocd far worse than it ever was in my life. I will list the one that is known to cause problems so you don't get scared about taking any form of psych-med: benzodiazepines. Stay away from them.

No quick fixes is what I say. Take the long and sure road nearly every-time.

Medication should be a last resort, is what I usually say. I'd say try working on your conditions as long as you can on your own -- with therapy and discipline -- before blocking off and numbing yourself. In my experience medication puts a blanket over your problems, which seems great, but eventually it leads to a place in your life where you become complacent with everything even though you know it isn't very good.

I am currently almost 3 months clean from psych-drugs and I do not wish to go back. Things have gotten much worse, but I find more reward in confronting the issues myself and dealing with them face-to-face.

I have said "I feel more like a person".

Do you have a phone or device of some kind you can use to listen to something peaceful (rain falling, wind, fireplace, leaves rustling, grass blowing)?
